title: The names
hookLine: Allah teaches Adam the names of all things, and the angels admit they know only what they were taught (2:31–33)
tomorrow: The one who would not bow

lines: A TODDLER POINTING: DOG, BALL, MOON.
cards: Moon. Every new word is a small victory, and the whole family cheers. Something enormous is happening: the world is splitting into things that can be told apart, held in the mind, talked about.
Once a child can say moon, they can ask where it goes in the daytime. Now God answers the angels. And the answer isn't strength, or goodness.

teach.h: HE TAUGHT ADAM ALL THE NAMES.
teach.b: Surah two, verse thirty-one, in Pickthall's words: “And He taught Adam all the names.” Then God sets the things before the angels: tell Me their names, if you're right.
The angels answer honestly: “We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us.” Then Adam is asked, and he names them, one by one. That's the answer to yesterday's question.
What makes this creature worth the risk? He can be taught.

teach.h: WE KNOW ONLY WHAT WE WERE TAUGHT.
teach.b: What were the names? The Qur'an doesn't say, and the commentators have their favorite answers. Some early authorities said everything, down to a bowl and a cooking pot.
Some said the names of the angels, or of Adam's own descendants. Some later thinkers read it as the gift of language itself: the power to tell one thing from another and know it.
A hadith in Bukhari, about the Day of Judgment, has people coming to Adam and listing what God gave him, and the names are on that list: He taught you the names of all things.
And look at the angels. They don't bluff. They say: we only know what we were taught.
To name a thing, you have to look at it long enough to tell it apart from everything else. Naming is noticing, made permanent.

how: Muslims often point to this passage as the root of Islam's regard for knowledge, and many teachers open lessons by recalling that God taught Adam the names.

games.q: you're one of the angels. God sets things before you and says: tell Me their names, if you're right. you don't know them. what do you say?
o: we know only what You taught us.
games.why: "We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us." then Adam named them.

practice: Look slowly around the room and name five things silently, staying with each one until you've really seen it: the color of a mug, the way the light sits on the wall.
Then close your eyes and name one thing you can hear, and one you can feel. If you pray, remember who, in the story, first taught the names.

wordCard.voice: The names. What God taught Adam, and what the angels didn't know: the first gift in the human story is words.

orig.note: Arabic: the names, plural of ism, name; in 2:31, al-asma'a kullaha, all the names.

carryVoice: Your line: to name is to notice. Knowing starts with looking closely. See you tomorrow.
